title: The art of paying attention
body:
There is a house on my street with a small blue chair on the porch. I have passed it almost every day for three years. Last Tuesday, for reasons I cannot explain, I noticed that one of its legs is shorter than the others. Someone has folded a piece of cardboard beneath it.

That piece of cardboard stayed with me all morning. I liked the thought of somebody sitting down, feeling the wobble, going inside for a solution. Not a new chair. Just something to make this chair work.

I tend to think of attention as a kind of effort. A thing you apply to a difficult book or a conversation in a loud room. But there is another sort that arrives when effort falls away. You miss your bus. Your phone runs out of battery. You sit on a wall for ten minutes with nothing to do, and the street begins to acquire details.

A delivery driver knows the name of the dog at number forty. The trees outside the pharmacy lean in different directions. Someone has been painting over the same patch of graffiti in increasingly inaccurate shades of beige.

None of this is useful, exactly. I do not come home improved by it. I just come home with a slightly different sense of where I live.

Yesterday the chair was gone. The cardboard was still there, a small square turning soft in the rain. I found myself hoping they were only painting it.

title: A room of ordinary things
body:
The first thing I unpacked was a cup with a crack in its handle. There were better cups in the same box. This one had come with me through four apartments, and I knew exactly how much tea to pour before it became too hot to hold.

For the first week the new room sounded wrong. My footsteps were too clear. There was nowhere for the noise to go. I put books on a shelf, a coat on the back of a chair, and a rug beneath the table. Slowly, the room learned to absorb me.

I used to save pictures of beautiful rooms. Rooms without chargers, receipts, drying socks. I still like looking at them, but I no longer confuse them with places I would want to spend a wet Sunday.

The table here has a slope. A pen will roll toward the window if you leave it alone. I have started using that end for the bowl of fruit. These are the arrangements that make a place yours: small accommodations nobody else would think to make.

This morning I stood in the kitchen with the cracked cup and watched someone across the street shake a blanket out of a window. For the first time, I did not feel as though I were visiting.

title: Taking the long way home
body:
The shortcut saves eleven minutes. I know because I measured it once, back when eleven minutes seemed like something worth recovering.

It runs behind the supermarket and along a wall without windows. The longer route goes past the allotments, over a small bridge, and through a street where somebody is always fixing a bicycle.

Last Thursday I took the long way. At the bridge, a man was lowering a bucket on a rope. I asked what he was doing. He said his granddaughter wanted to know what lived in the water. In the bucket there was a leaf and something small that moved too quickly to identify.

We looked at it for a while. Then he tipped the bucket back.

I got home eleven minutes later than I could have. The washing was still there. So was the email. I made dinner and thought about the small thing in the bucket, which had briefly been the center of three people’s afternoon.

title: What we keep
body:
I own a key that opens nothing I can remember. It has lived in the same dish for so long that throwing it away now would feel like making a decision about the past.

There is also a bus ticket, a smooth stone, and a photograph in which everyone is looking in a different direction. The photograph is objectively bad. It is my favorite one from that summer.

When I clean, I make two piles. The useful things and the other things. The useful pile is easy: batteries, scissors, a cable I still need. The other pile requires a whole afternoon.

I am learning that keeping something does not always mean I want to go back. Sometimes it means I was there, and I would like a small, unreasonable piece of evidence.

I put the key back in the dish. Perhaps next time.

title: In praise of unfinished books
body:
On the shelf beside my bed are six books I have not finished. One has been there for two years. The bookmark is a receipt from a restaurant that has since closed.

I used to turn reading into a contract. If I began, I had to finish. This produced some very long evenings and an unreasonable dislike of perfectly good writers.

Now I try to leave a book without judging it. Perhaps it is the wrong week. Perhaps I need a story and it wants to offer an argument. Perhaps I simply do not like it.

The strange thing is that I remember some unfinished books more clearly than the ones I read to the end. A scene, a sentence, the particular light in a room. Enough came across.

Last night I picked up the book with the restaurant receipt. I read three pages. It was suddenly exactly what I wanted.

title: The weather inside a song
body:
A song came on in the grocery store, and I was nineteen again, sitting in a car outside a house I have not seen in years.

I could remember the dashboard. A little dust where the glass met the plastic. The heater smelled faintly of something burnt. We were waiting for a friend who always said he would be two minutes.

I cannot deliberately remember that afternoon. If you asked me about it yesterday, I would have said there was nothing to tell. But the first few notes returned the whole thing, including the feeling of having nowhere else I needed to be.

The song ended. I was holding a bag of onions.

I bought them, went home, and played the song again. It was still a good song. The car did not come back.
